subtitulo: PASOK, structural funds and entry into the euro: twenty years building the crisis (1981–2001)

coda.heading: Coda for the trip: what to look for

items.text: In Athens, the metro. It was built in the nineties with European financing and is excellent: clean, punctual, and with archaeological display cases in several stations — Syntagma, Monastiraki, Acropolis — exhibiting what was found during the excavation. It is a good symbol of the period: European infrastructure that, in digging, runs into Antiquity and folds it into the daily commute. Notice how it is presented.

In Corfu, ask about the European funds: the airport, the cruise port, the roads. And ask who manages them and who benefited. On an island that lives off tourism, infrastructure financed by cohesion funds increases the capacity to receive visitors — that is, it deepens the specialization rather than diversifying it. It is the same debate as the canon: public investment can reinforce the very dependency it was meant to offset.

closing: Notice too the Eleftherios Venizelos airport, opened in 2001, and the highways: they belong to this period. And contrast that with the state of public schools and hospitals if you get the chance to see them. That asymmetry between first-rate transport infrastructure and strained social services is the portrait of the model.

sections.heading: The Change: inclusion by way of the state
paragraphs: PASOK won the elections of October 1981 with the slogan ALLAGI, the Change, and with a platform that combined socialism, Third-Worldism and nationalism: withdrawal from NATO, a challenge to the European Community, American bases out. It fulfilled none of the three. Andreas Papandreou — a trained economist with an academic career in the United States, son of the prime minister toppled in 1965 — governed for eleven of the following thirteen years.

What he did do was a genuine social transformation, and it deserves recognition before criticism. The national health system was created in 1983. The Resistance was legally recognized in 1982. A 1983 reform of family law abolished the dowry as a legal institution, established equality between spouses, legalized civil marriage and no-fault divorce; abortion was decriminalized in 1986. For Greek women, that legislation changed life more than anything else that happened in the century, and it dismantled much of the legal regime underpinning the honor economy described in dispatch 10. Pensions were extended to the peasantry, real wages rose, access to university expanded.

And all of it was done, essentially, through the state as employer and as payer. The incorporation of the historically excluded sectors — the losers of the civil war, the provinces, the peasantry — was carried out through public employment, contract regularizations, early pensions and transfers. It is the machine of dispatch 16 operating at massive scale, and with a democratic legitimacy it had never had before. The right, when it returned to power, ran it the same way.

The fiscal result was predictable: Greek public debt rose from moderate levels in the early eighties to more than one hundred percent of output by the mid-nineties. And the political result was a profound depoliticization of the relationship with the state: not a citizen with rights, but a beneficiary with a contact. In Peru it's called vara; in Greece, meson.

sections.heading: The European funds: the periphery as recipient
paragraphs: From 1981 on, and above all from the Community Support Frameworks of 1989 and 1994, Greece received substantial, sustained European transfers: structural, cohesion and agricultural funds, which in some years amounted to several points of annual output. With them, highways, airports, the Athens metro and bridges were built — the Rio-Antirrio bridge, opened in 2004 — and much of the country's infrastructure was modernized.

Reading these funds correctly requires precision and avoids two common mistakes. They were not charity: cohesion policy exists because a single market with very different currencies and productivities produces divergence, and the transfers are the compensating mechanism that makes integration politically sustainable. Nor were they neutral: much of the spending went toward physical infrastructure rather than productive capacities, technical education or innovation, partly because infrastructure is easier to tender, to inaugurate and to turn into clientele. Greece ended the nineties with excellent roads and a productive structure practically as dependent as when it began: tourism, maritime transport, agriculture, a large public sector and very little export industry.

The Peruvian comparison is direct, and it applies to the debate over mining canon revenue and royalties. A flow of resources that reaches a territory without transforming its productive matrix builds visible works and creates no capacity. Peruvian municipalities with abundant canon revenue, with inaugurated public works alongside stagnant social indicators, replicate, on another scale, exactly the Greek problem of the nineties. In both cases the problem is not corruption — which exists — but something harder: infrastructure is a necessary but not sufficient condition for development, and it is far easier to spend on than capacities are to build.

sections.heading: 2001: entering the euro and accounting as politics
paragraphs: The strategic objective of Greek policy in the nineties was entry into the single currency. Simitis, prime minister from 1996, ran an adjustment and stabilization program that brought inflation down from double digits to European levels. Greece did not meet the criteria in 1998 alongside the first eleven countries, and entered on January 1, 2001.

Entering the euro had a sound logic for a country like Greece: it eliminated exchange-rate risk, imported German monetary credibility and drastically reduced the cost of debt. In 1993 the Greek state paid interest rates far above German ones; by the mid-2000s it was paying almost the same. A country with debt above one hundred percent of output saw its interest burden fall spectacularly. In the short run, it was a huge success.

And it contained three time bombs. The first: markets stopped distinguishing between Greek and German debt, that is, they stopped pricing risk, which let a state and a private sector that had solved no structural problem borrow cheaply. The second: with the possibility of devaluation gone, the only remaining path of adjustment to a loss of competitiveness was INTERNAL DEVALUATION, that is, falling wages and prices, which is socially devastating and politically almost impossible. The third: the public accounts presented were, in part, fiction. In 2004 the Greek government itself admitted that deficit figures had been systematically understated, and in 2009 the revision revealed that the real deficit was on the order of double the declared figure or more. It also came to light that swap operations with investment banks had been used to defer debt off the balance sheet.

It's worth not reducing this to a story of Greek cheats, because that would be false through incompleteness. The understatement of deficits was known and tolerated by European institutions, which had a political objective — the expansion of the single currency — that outranked statistical rigor; other countries practiced creative accounting too; and the design of the monetary union deliberately lacked mechanisms for joint bank supervision, deposit insurance and a sovereign lender of last resort — that is, everything a monetary union needs in order not to break apart. Greece lied about its accounts and Europe built a currency without architecture. Both things produced 2010.

sections.heading: Peruvian mirror: the same years, a different adjustment
paragraphs: While Greece was making its European convergence, Peru was carrying out its own adjustment with comparable instruments and opposite political results.

The country was emerging from the hyperinflation of 1988–1990 — with cumulative inflation difficult to express in comprehensible figures — from the collapse of the state and from war. The 1990 stabilization program, trade liberalization, the massive privatizations of 1991–1997, the new 1993 constitution with its economic regime and its stability contracts, and reinsertion into the international financial system produced genuine, lasting macroeconomic stability: Peru has had since then one of the lowest inflation rates and one of the most manageable public debts in the region.

The decisive difference is political. Greece carried out its adjustment within a democratic framework and with an integration objective that expanded rights; Peru carried it out with a self-coup in April 1992, a regime that dismantled institutional checks, and an apparatus of corruption and media manipulation whose scale only became known with the vladivideos in 2000. The result is that in Peru macroeconomic stability became linked in collective memory to an authoritarian regime, and the subsequent economic debate remained trapped in that association for thirty years: defending fiscal discipline reads as defending Fujimorismo, and criticizing it reads as threatening stability. Greece never carried that fusion, and that is why it could discuss its economic model in the 2010s in properly political terms.
The general observation: who carries out the adjustment, and under what regime, matters, because it determines what can be discussed for the following generation.

sections.heading: Resonances 2024–2026
paragraphs: Two living legacies. The first: the architecture of the euro was partially corrected after 2012 — banking union, the European Stability Mechanism, the European Central Bank's commitment to do whatever it takes, and since 2020 the recovery fund with common debt issuance, which broke a founding taboo. In other words, the monetary union acquired, late and in fits and starts, part of the institutions it had lacked. Greece paid a good share of the cost of that learning process.

The second: European funds remain the principal instrument of Greek public investment, now via the post-pandemic recovery plan, and the debate over their absorption and the quality of that spending was replayed in 2024–2026 in the same terms as the nineties. Nothing ages less than a debate about execution capacity.

And a methodological warning before the next dispatch. About the Greek crisis there are two complete, mutually exclusive narratives: that of a country that lived beyond its means and was rescued, and that of a country sacrificed to save French and German banks exposed to its debt. Both contain true facts, and both deliberately omit what does not suit them. The next dispatch will try to hold both sets of facts at once, which is the only way to understand why the crisis was so destructive and why neither narrative produced a way out.
